title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals
description: Change of variables in double and triple integrals (OpenStax 5.7, a 40 minute class): watch a small du dv piece be stretched into its image to see the Jacobian, then work many examples: parallelograms, a hard integrand, ellipses, curved boundaries, triple integrals, and the cylindrical and spherical factors as special cases.

steps.label: Substitution, Again
steps.subtitle: Why change variables?
steps.bodyHtml:
One variable: to compute \(\displaystyle\int_0^2 x\,e^{x^2}\,dx\) we substitute \(u=x^2\). The rule is

$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\int_c^d f(g(u))\,g'(u)\,du,\qquad x=g(u).$$
Evaluate \(\int_0^2 xe^{x^2}dx\) with \(u=x^2\)\(du=2x\,dx\), limits \(0\to4\): \(\tfrac12\int_0^4e^u\,du=\tfrac12(e^4-1)\).
What does the factor \(g'(u)=\dfrac{dx}{du}\) measure?How much the substitution stretches length: a piece of length \(du\) becomes a piece of length \(g'(u)\,du\).
In two variables, a change of variables stretches area. We already met one case. What is it?Polar coordinates: \(dA=r\,dr\,d\theta\). The factor \(r\) is the area stretch factor. Today we find it for any change of variables.
Two reasons to change variables(1) to turn an awkward region (a parallelogram, an ellipse, a region between curves) into a rectangle or disk; (2) to simplify the integrand (e.g. \(e^{x^2-y^2}\) becomes \(e^{uv}\)). Often both.

Plan: transformations and their images (2 steps), the Jacobian and the theorem (2 steps), then examples: parallelograms, a hard integrand, ellipses, curved boundaries, triple integrals, and a link back to cylindrical and spherical coordinates.

steps.label: Transformations
steps.subtitle: Images of regions (Examples 5.65, 5.66, Checkpoint 5.43)
steps.bodyHtml:
A transformation \(T(u,v)=(x,y)\), with \(x=g(u,v)\) and \(y=h(u,v)\), sends a region \(S\) in the \(uv\)-plane onto a region \(R\) in the \(xy\)-plane. It is \(C^1\) if \(g,h\) have continuous first partials, and one-to-one if \(T(u_1,v_1)=T(u_2,v_2)\) forces \((u_1,v_1)=(u_2,v_2)\). Then \(T^{-1}:R\to S\) exists.

Example 1 (polar). \(T(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta)\) on \(S=\{0
The image \(R\)The quarter of the unit disk in the first quadrant.
One-to-one on \(S\)?Yes. If \(r_1\cos\theta_1=r_2\cos\theta_2\) and \(r_1\sin\theta_1=r_2\sin\theta_2\), dividing gives \(\cot\theta_1=\cot\theta_2\), so \(\theta_1=\theta_2\) on \([0,\tfrac\pi2]\), then \(r_1=r_2\). (On \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\) it would fail: \(\theta=0\) and \(2\pi\) give the same point.)
The inverse\(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), \(\ \theta=\tan^{-1}(y/x)\).

Example 2. \(T(u,v)=(u+v,\ 3v)\) on the rectangle \(S=[0,1]\times[0,2]\).

Images of the four vertices \((0,0),(1,0),(0,2),(1,2)\)\((0,0),\ (1,0),\ (2,6),\ (3,6)\).
The image \(R\)The parallelogram with those vertices (a linear map sends line segments to line segments).
Solve for the inverse\(v=y/3\) and \(u=x-v=x-y/3\). A formula exists, so \(T\) is one-to-one.

Example 3. \(T(u,v)=(u^2-v^2,\ uv)\) on the triangle \(S\) with vertices \((0,0),(0,1),(1,1)\). Send each side across.

Side \(u=0\), \(0\le v\le1\)\((-v^2,0)\): the segment from \((0,0)\) to \((-1,0)\) on the \(x\)-axis.
Side \(u=v\), \(0\le u\le1\)\((0,u^2)\): the segment from \((0,0)\) up to \((0,1)\) on the \(y\)-axis.
Side \(v=1\), \(0\le u\le1\)\((u^2-1,\ u)\): here \(x=y^2-1\), the arc of a parabola from \((-1,0)\) to \((0,1)\).
So \(R\) isthe region bounded by the \(x\)-axis, the \(y\)-axis and that parabola arc: the boundary of \(S\) maps onto the boundary of \(R\).

steps.label: Explore: How a Transformation Stretches Area
steps.subtitle: The factor in front of du dv
steps.bodyHtml:
Here \(T(u,v)=(u^2-v^2,\ uv)\) on the unit square. The red piece \(\Delta u\times\Delta v\) on the left becomes the curved red piece on the right. The dashed parallelogram is the straight-sided approximation. Drag the corner of the piece, then shrink it.

Shrink the piece. What happens to the ratio \(|J|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v\) over the true area?It tends to \(1\). So \(\Delta A\approx|J(u,v)|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v\), and in the limit \(dA=|J|\,du\,dv\).
Drag the piece from near the origin to near \((1,1)\). What does \(J\) do?It grows from about \(0\) to \(4\): \(J=2u^2+2v^2\). The same \(\Delta u\Delta v\) piece is blown up much more near \((1,1)\).
Why does the theorem ask for \(J\neq0\) in the interior of \(S\)?Where \(J=0\) the map crushes area to zero (here at \((0,0)\)). The image of the whole square then has area \(\iint_S|J|\,du\,dv=\iint_S(2u^2+2v^2)\,du\,dv=\tfrac43\).

steps.label: The Jacobian
steps.subtitle: Definition, Theorem 5.14, and a drill
steps.bodyHtml:
The Jacobian of \(T(u,v)=(x,y)\) is the determinant

$$J(u,v)=\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\begin{vmatrix}\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\[2mm]\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}=\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}-\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}.$$

It is the area of the parallelogram spanned by \(\vec r_u\,\Delta u\) and \(\vec r_v\,\Delta v\) (the dashed one in the picture), per unit \(\Delta u\Delta v\).

Theorem 5.14. Let \(T\) be a one-to-one \(C^1\) transformation, with \(J\neq0\) on the interior of \(S\), mapping \(S\) onto \(R\). If \(f\) is continuous on \(R\), then

$$\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_S f\big(g(u,v),h(u,v)\big)\,\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,du\,dv.$$

In practice: replace \(dx\,dy\) by \(|J|\,du\,dv\), write \(x,y\) in terms of \(u,v\), and change the limits. Note the absolute value.

Drill. Compute \(J\) for each map.

Polar: \(x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta\) (Example 5.67)\(\begin{vmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta\end{vmatrix}=r\cos^2\theta+r\sin^2\theta=r\). So \(dA=r\,dr\,d\theta\).
\(x=u^2-v^2,\ y=uv\) (Example 5.68)\(\begin{vmatrix}2u&-2v\\v&u\end{vmatrix}=2u^2+2v^2\)
\(x=u+v,\ y=3v\)\(\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\0&3\end{vmatrix}=3\). A linear map has a constant \(J\) (the determinant of its matrix).
\(x=3u,\ y=2v\) (scaling)\(\begin{vmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{vmatrix}=6\)
\(x=e^u\cos v,\ y=e^u\sin v\)\(\begin{vmatrix}e^u\cos v&-e^u\sin v\\ e^u\sin v&e^u\cos v\end{vmatrix}=e^{2u}\)
\(u=xy,\ v=y/x\), the Jacobian \(\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\) of the inverse\(\begin{vmatrix}y&x\\-y/x^2&1/x\end{vmatrix}=\dfrac yx+\dfrac yx=\dfrac{2y}{x}=2v\). Keep this one for Example 7.

steps.label: Strategy, and Parallelograms
steps.subtitle: Examples 4 and 5
steps.bodyHtml:
Strategy. (1) Sketch \(R\) and write the equations of its boundary curves. (2) Choose \(u,v\) from the boundary curves (make them constant on the sides) or from the integrand. (3) Find the region \(S\) in the \(uv\)-plane. (4) Solve for \(x,y\) and compute \(J\). (5) Rewrite the integrand. (6) Replace \(dA\) by \(|J|\,du\,dv\) and integrate.

Example 4 (Example 5.70). \(\displaystyle\iint_R(x-y)\,dA\), where \(R\) is the parallelogram with vertices \((1,2),(3,4),(6,5),(4,3)\).

Equations of the four sides\((1,2)\)-\((3,4)\) and \((4,3)\)-\((6,5)\): \(x-y=-1\) and \(x-y=1\). \(\ (1,2)\)-\((4,3)\) and \((3,4)\)-\((6,5)\): \(x-3y=-5\) and \(x-3y=-9\).
Choose \(u,v\) and find \(S\)\(u=x-y\), \(v=x-3y\). Then \(-1\le u\le1\) and \(-9\le v\le-5\): a rectangle.
Solve for \(x,y\); find \(|J|\)\(u-v=2y\), so \(y=\tfrac{u-v}2\) and \(x=u+y=\tfrac{3u-v}2\). \(\ J=\begin{vmatrix}3/2&-1/2\\1/2&-1/2\end{vmatrix}=-\tfrac12\), \(|J|=\tfrac12\).
The integral\(\displaystyle\int_{-9}^{-5}\!\int_{-1}^{1}u\cdot\tfrac12\,du\,dv=\int_{-9}^{-5}\Big[\tfrac{u^2}4\Big]_{-1}^{1}dv=0\).
Is \(0\) believable?Yes: the integrand \(x-y=u\) changes sign across the line \(x-y=0\), and \(R\) is symmetric about that line in the \(u\)-direction. Contributions cancel.

Example 5. \(\iint_R(x+y)\,dA\), where \(R\) is bounded by \(x+y=1,\ x+y=3,\ x-2y=0,\ x-2y=3\). Here is the map from \(S\) to \(R\) (the ratio does not change from place to place).

Choose \(u,v\); find \(S\)\(u=x+y\in[1,3]\), \(v=x-2y\in[0,3]\). A rectangle again.
Solve for \(x,y\); find \(|J|\)\(u-v=3y\), so \(y=\tfrac{u-v}3\), \(x=u-y=\tfrac{2u+v}3\). \(\ J=\begin{vmatrix}2/3&1/3\\1/3&-1/3\end{vmatrix}=-\tfrac19-\tfrac29=-\tfrac13\).
The integral\(\displaystyle\int_0^3\!\int_1^3u\cdot\tfrac13\,du\,dv=\tfrac13\cdot3\cdot\tfrac{9-1}{2}=4\).
Check with the area of \(R\)\(\text{Area}(R)=\iint_S\tfrac13\,du\,dv=\tfrac13\cdot2\cdot3=2\), which is also what the picture suggests.

steps.label: A Substitution that Tames the Integrand
steps.subtitle: Example 6 (Example 5.71)
steps.bodyHtml:
Evaluate \(\displaystyle\iint_R(x-y)\,e^{x^2-y^2}\,dA\), where \(R\) is the region bounded by the lines \(x+y=1\) and \(x+y=3\) and the curves \(x^2-y^2=-1\) and \(x^2-y^2=1\).

Written in \(x\) and \(y\) this is hopeless: the region has hyperbolas for sides and the integrand has no elementary antiderivative in either variable. Factor the exponent.

\(x^2-y^2=(x-y)(x+y)\). Choose \(u,v\)\(u=x-y\), \(v=x+y\). Then \(x^2-y^2=uv\) and the integrand is \(u\,e^{uv}\).
The region \(S\)\(1\le v\le3\), and \(-1\le uv\le1\) means \(-\tfrac1v\le u\le\tfrac1v\).
Solve for \(x,y\); find \(|J|\)\(x=\tfrac{u+v}2\), \(y=\tfrac{v-u}2\). \(\ J=\begin{vmatrix}1/2&1/2\\-1/2&1/2\end{vmatrix}=\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12\).
Set up\(\displaystyle\iint_R=\tfrac12\int_1^3\int_{-1/v}^{1/v}u\,e^{uv}\,du\,dv\).
Inner integral (by parts in \(u\), \(v\) held fixed)\(\displaystyle\int u e^{uv}du=e^{uv}\Big(\tfrac uv-\tfrac1{v^2}\Big)\). From \(-\tfrac1v\) to \(\tfrac1v\): \(e\cdot0-e^{-1}\Big(-\tfrac1{v^2}-\tfrac1{v^2}\Big)=\dfrac{2}{e\,v^2}\).
Outer integral\(\displaystyle\tfrac12\int_1^3\frac{2}{e\,v^2}\,dv=\frac1e\Big[-\frac1v\Big]_1^3=\frac1e\cdot\frac23=\frac{2}{3e}\approx0.245\).

steps.label: Ellipses: Scale First
steps.subtitle: Examples 7 and 8
steps.bodyHtml:
Example 7. Area of an ellipse. \(R:\ \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}\le1\).

Which \(u,v\) turn the ellipse into a disk?\(u=\tfrac xa\), \(v=\tfrac yb\), so \(x=au\), \(y=bv\), and \(S\) is the unit disk \(u^2+v^2\le1\).
\(J\)\(\begin{vmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{vmatrix}=ab\)
The area\(\iint_R1\,dA=\iint_S ab\,du\,dv=ab\cdot\text{Area}(S)=\pi ab\).

Example 8. Two changes in a row. \(\displaystyle\iint_R\Big(\frac{x^2}9+\frac{y^2}4\Big)dA\), where \(R\) is the region \(\dfrac{x^2}9+\dfrac{y^2}4\le1\).

First change: \(a=3\), \(b=2\)\(x=3u,\ y=2v\), \(|J|=6\), \(S\) the unit disk. The integrand becomes \(u^2+v^2\), so \(\displaystyle\iint_R=6\iint_{u^2+v^2\le1}(u^2+v^2)\,dA\).
Second change: polar in the \(uv\)-plane\(u=r\cos\theta\), \(v=r\sin\theta\), \(dA=r\,dr\,d\theta\): \(\displaystyle6\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^1r^2\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta\).
Evaluate\(6\cdot2\pi\cdot\tfrac14=3\pi\).
Sanity check: at most what could the answer be?The integrand is \(\le1\) on \(R\), so the integral is at most \(\text{Area}(R)=6\pi\). We got \(3\pi\), half of that: the average value of \(\tfrac{x^2}9+\tfrac{y^2}4\) is \(\tfrac12\). Plausible.

steps.label: Curved Boundaries
steps.subtitle: Example 9: when the inverse is awkward
steps.bodyHtml:
Let \(R\) be the region in the first quadrant bounded by \(xy=1,\ xy=4,\ y=x,\ y=4x\). Compute its area and \(\displaystyle\iint_R(x^2+y^2)\,dA\).

Choose \(u,v\) so that each side has one constant\(u=xy\), \(v=\tfrac yx\). Then \(1\le u\le4\) and \(1\le v\le4\): a square in the \(uv\)-plane.
Solving for \(x,y\) is messy: \(x=\sqrt{u/v},\ y=\sqrt{uv}\). What is an easier route to \(J\)?Use the Jacobian of the inverse: \(\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\dfrac{1}{\partial(u,v)/\partial(x,y)}\). From the drill, \(\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}=2v\), so \(\left|\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\dfrac1{2v}\).
Area of \(R\)\(\displaystyle\int_1^4\!\int_1^4\frac1{2v}\,du\,dv=\tfrac32\ln4=3\ln2\approx2.08\).
The integrand \(x^2+y^2\) in \(u,v\)\(x^2=\tfrac uv\) and \(y^2=uv\), so \(x^2+y^2=\tfrac uv+uv\).
The integral\(\displaystyle\int_1^4\!\int_1^4\Big(\frac uv+uv\Big)\frac1{2v}\,du\,dv=\frac12\int_1^4u\,du\int_1^4\Big(\frac1{v^2}+1\Big)dv=\frac12\cdot\frac{15}2\cdot\frac{15}4=\frac{225}{16}\).

Rule used: \(\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\cdot\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}=1\), the two-variable version of \(\dfrac{dx}{du}\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx}=1\). Use whichever direction is easier to compute.

steps.label: Triple Integrals
steps.subtitle: Theorem 5.15, Examples 10 and 11
steps.bodyHtml:
Theorem 5.15. If \(T(u,v,w)=(x,y,z)\) is a one-to-one \(C^1\) map of \(G\) onto \(R\) with nonzero Jacobian, then

$$\iiint_RF(x,y,z)\,dV=\iiint_GF(g,h,k)\left|\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw,\qquad \frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\begin{vmatrix}x_u&x_v&x_w\\y_u&y_v&y_w\\z_u&z_v&z_w\end{vmatrix}.$$

Example 10 (Example 5.73). \(\displaystyle\int_0^3\!\int_0^4\!\int_{y/2}^{y/2+1}\Big(x+\frac z3\Big)\,dx\,dy\,dz\), using \(u=\dfrac{2x-y}2,\ v=\dfrac y2,\ w=\dfrac z3\).

Solve for \(x,y,z\)\(x=u+v,\quad y=2v,\quad z=3w\).
The new limits\(\tfrac y2\le x\le\tfrac y2+1\) means \(0\le u\le1\). \(\ 0\le y\le4\) gives \(0\le v\le2\). \(\ 0\le z\le3\) gives \(0\le w\le1\). A box.
\(J\)\(\begin{vmatrix}1&1&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{vmatrix}=6\) (triangular: multiply the diagonal).
The integrand and the value\(x+\tfrac z3=u+v+w\). \(\ 6\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\int_0^2\!\int_0^1(u+v+w)\,du\,dv\,dw=6(1+2+1)=24\).

Example 11. Volume of an ellipsoid. \(E:\ \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}+\dfrac{z^2}{c^2}\le1\).

The map\(x=au,\ y=bv,\ z=cw\) turns \(E\) into the unit ball \(u^2+v^2+w^2\le1\), and \(J=abc\).
The volume\(\iiint_E1\,dV=abc\cdot\text{Vol}(\text{unit ball})=\tfrac43\pi\,abc\).
Check: \(a=b=c=r\)\(\tfrac43\pi r^3\), the volume of a ball. For a spheroid \(\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{z^2}{c^2}\le1\) it gives \(\tfrac43\pi a^2c\).

steps.label: Cylindrical and Spherical: Special Cases
steps.subtitle: Example 12 (Example 5.72)
steps.bodyHtml:
Last lesson we found \(dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz\) and \(dV=\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\varphi\) by drawing a small coordinate box and measuring its edges. The Jacobian gives the same factors from a determinant.

Cylindrical: \(x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta,\ z=z\). Compute \(\dfrac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(r,\theta,z)}\)\(\begin{vmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta&0\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot(r\cos^2\theta+r\sin^2\theta)=r\). So \(dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz\).
Spherical: \(x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\ y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\ z=\rho\cos\varphi\). Write the \(3\times3\) matrix in the order \((\rho,\theta,\varphi)\)\(\begin{bmatrix}\sin\varphi\cos\theta&-\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta&\rho\cos\varphi\cos\theta\\ \sin\varphi\sin\theta&\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta&\rho\cos\varphi\sin\theta\\ \cos\varphi&0&-\rho\sin\varphi\end{bmatrix}\)
Its determinant (expand along the bottom row)\(\det=-\rho^2\sin\varphi\). The sign depends on the order of the variables, which is why the theorem uses \(|J|\): \(\ |J|=\rho^2\sin\varphi\), since \(\sin\varphi\ge0\) on \([0,\pi]\).
Which Example above is also a "special case"?Example 7 and Example 11 (the scalings \(x=au\), \(x=au,y=bv,z=cw\)) and Example 1 (polar). Every coordinate system is a change of variables with its own Jacobian.

steps.label: Summary
steps.subtitle: The one-page version
steps.bodyHtml:
Jacobian\(\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=x_uy_v-x_vy_u\). Area stretch factor: \(dA=|J|\,du\,dv\). Linear maps have constant \(J\) (the determinant).
Theorem\(\iint_Rf\,dA=\iint_Sf(g,h)\,|J|\,du\,dv\), and likewise in 3D with a \(3\times3\) determinant. Needs one-to-one, \(C^1\), \(J\neq0\) inside.
Choosing \(u,v\)Make each boundary curve have one constant (\(x\pm y\), \(xy\), \(y/x\), \(x/a\)), or simplify the integrand (\(x^2-y^2=uv\)).
Inverse trick\(\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\Big(\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\Big)^{-1}\). Use it when solving for \(x,y\) is messy.
Answers today\(0\), \(4\), \(\tfrac2{3e}\), \(\pi ab\), \(3\pi\), \(3\ln2\), \(\tfrac{225}{16}\), \(24\), \(\tfrac43\pi abc\).

Homework: OpenStax 5.7 Checkpoints 5.43 to 5.48 and exercises on images of the unit square (356 to 361), Jacobians (378 to 387), integrals over parallelograms and trapezoids (390 to 397), triple integrals (404, 405) and the spheroid volume (412, 413). Next: line integrals.
